title: The Thing with Cheating
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart argues that cheating persists in classrooms not because students lack rules but because they lack internalized reasons to care about learning itself, and he lays out three "realizations" he works to cultivate to make cheating less appealing. The first is that the point of school is growth toward mastery, balanced with rest, enjoyment, and relationships — a message he says must be repeated hundreds of times a year, not stated once. The second is that learning toward mastery is intrinsically more enjoyable than disengagement, a case he says he can only make persuasively while students are physically in his classroom. The third is that learning is something only the learner can do for themselves — no teacher or peer can supply the effort. He closes by noting that this framework predates ChatGPT entirely, since the same dynamics were true with essay-mills a decade ago and in the 1950s, making the point that cheating is a timeless motivational problem rather than a new technological one.
points: Stuart's causal claim — cheating is a rational trade of a short-term positive (a grade) for a long-term negative (lost learning, false feedback, character erosion) — reframes academic dishonesty as a motivation problem rather than a discipline problem.

His three realizations (mastery is the point of school; learning is intrinsically enjoyable; only the learner can do the learning) function as a repeatable script teachers can use across the year, not a one-time lecture.

He's explicit that his classroom influence over these beliefs is "really big" while students are present but "drops precipitously" once they leave — a candid admission of the limits of any single teacher's reach.
By explicitly noting the argument predates ChatGPT and essay mills alike, Stuart resists treating AI-enabled cheating as a categorically new problem requiring a new solution.
quotes: The thing with cheating in school is that it trades a short-term "positive" (completion of an assignment; better grade) for a long-term negative (lost learning opportunity; inaccurate feedback on learning; degradation of character).
In my classroom practice, the surest way to decrease student cheating is to give my students regular opportunities to think on these things.

This is something to communicate not once or twice, but rather hundreds and hundreds of times per class per school year. Each teacher needs to articulate this in their own way, but the point — of art, of phys ed, of science, of poetry — is GROWTH TOWARD MASTERY.

Again, casting this vision and creating this culture is my job during my class time. Many other factors influence the degree to which a student believes these things, but the only factor I control is my influence.
Once students leave my class, my influence drops precipitously. But while they're with me, my influence is really big.

If we teachers grow in our attention to cultivating these key realizations, suddenly cheating becomes much less of a problem. It doesn't vanish — I have academic dishonesty cases every school year — but it does sink to the background where it belongs.

What I've said above is true in a world with ChatGPT just as it was true in a world with essay-writing services ten years ago, just as it was true in the 1950s and 1850s and before. These are timeless realities.
